title: MA8-08749
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: I will render my oral decision regarding the identity of XXXX XXXX XXX XXXXXXXX, file MA8-08749.
On the issue of citizenship, Mr. XXXXXXXX was born in XXXX, Jordan, on XXXX, 1989.

Mr. XXXXXXXX wrote in his application for a study permit, made outside Canada and signed on XXXX, 2008, that he was a Jordanian citizen. He referred to a passport number, which is listed on his application for a study permit as XXXX, and this passport was valid until XXXX, 2009.
He was 18 years old when he made this application for a study permit outside Canada. He stated that the information provided in that document was complete, true and correct.

In Exhibit P-8, which was submitted by the claimant and refers to his passport, there are two different passports. We find the one that is identified as XXXXXX, which he referred to in his application for a study permit made outside Canada. That passport, which was issued by the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, states that the claimant was born in XXXX. The passport was issued on XXXX, 2004, and was valid until XXXX, 2009. It bears national identity number XXXXXX.

According to Mr. XXXXXXX testimony this morning, a few days later he obtained what he considers to be a temporary passport with the number XXXXX, which was issued by Jordan on XXXX, 2008, and is valid until XXXX, 2013. This passport is also part of Exhibit P-8. According to the claimant, he is no longer a Jordanian citizen; he pointed out that this passport does not bear the national identity number.
It is true that I do not find a national identity number on this photocopy of the passport when I read it.

In his Personal Information Form (PIF), the claimant states that his parents are Palestinian citizens. Palestine is still not recognized internationally as an independent state and, in practice, this means that his parents are stateless.

However, during his interview with an immigration officer on XXXX, 2008, Mr. XXXXX told the officer that his father and mother were Jordanian citizens and that they obtained their Jordanian citizenship before he was born-so before 1989.

In the immigration documents under Exhibit A-2, in his passport-which appears as XXXXX and was issued on XXXX, 2008-we learn that Mr. XXXXXX was issued a visa in XXXX, Jordan, and that the Canadian visa was issued on XXXX, 2008. The visa was valid until XXXX, 2009, with multiple entries, student category. That visa makes reference to passport number XXXX-the passport issued on XXXX, 2008, which does not have a national identity number.

When we read the documents regarding the visa file, we find that the immigration officer who reviewed Mr. XXXXXXX application for a study permit stated that he was born in XXXX, but that he spent all his life in XXXX; that his father is a XXXX, a businessman involved in XXXXXX- XXXXX XXXX -and has been in business for 10 years or more; and that his mother XXXXXXXX XXXX. So it is indicated that the parents are XXXX with their own businesses, and there is an analysis of the parents' financial assets. The immigration officer states [translation] "that I am not convinced that Mr. XXXXXX will return to XXXX, one of the regions with the most problems," [English in original] "one of the more troubled regions of the west bank."

However, the claimant, Mr. XXXXXX, told the visa officer that he would return, since he is an only child and he has to take care of his parents. The visa officer also indicated that his father and his father's partner have other assets, as they also own land.
The visa officer's decision was taken "in light of his full Jordanian nationality," [translation] "the risk of a successful claim for refugee protection is greatly diminished."

These are very particular circumstances; the claimant before me presented documents to Canadian authorities in Jordan in order to obtain a visa to study in Canada. In these documents, he stated that he is a Jordanian citizen. The passport with the national identity number was valid until XXXX 2009.

It seems clear to me that the authorities in Jordan approved the application for a study permit based on this information and because they were convinced that, since he had full Jordanian citizenship, the risk of the claimant being granted refugee status in Canada was greatly diminished.

My role is to ascertain whether there is any possibility of persecution in the future. At the start of the hearing this morning, I asked whether the claimant was making a refugee protection claim against Jordan. There is no indication to that effect in the PIF. So the question is whether the claimant is a Jordanian citizen or not.

There are contradictions between the fact that, in his XXXX, 2008, application for a study permit, he states that he is a Jordanian citizen, and the fact that today he states that he is no longer a Jordanian citizen.

The documentary evidence indicates that Jordan issues passports to three categories of Palestinians: "Jordanian citizens of Palestinian origin who can obtain five-year passports with national identity numbers."1 It is clear that the claimant has already obtained a passport with a national identity number and it is clear that he claimed to be a Jordanian citizen.

However, he told me that he has lost his citizenship. He referred to a document for which a translation was submitted this morning: the bridge crossing card. He presented me the passport that he obtained after applying to study, which does not have a national identity number.

The documentary evidence indicates, particularly under tab 3.92 of the national documentation package, that more than half of Jordan`s population is of Palestinian origin. Over half of the 6.3 million, as indicated on page 1; with the exception of people from Gaza, the vast majority of people of Palestinian origin have Jordanian citizenship.

That being said, the same document also states that, between 2004 and 2008, Jordan revoked the citizenship of thousands of its citizens of Palestinian origin. According to Human Rights Watch, the cases that they have analyzed indicate that citizenship was revoked arbitrarily and in violation of the Jordanian nationality law of 1954.

It is also stated that this can happen without warning when someone tries to renew a passport. This document states that this action by Jordan contravenes many rights, including rights that are recognized in international conventions, including the 2004 Arab Charter on Human Rights, which recognizes citizenship rights.

This law on Jordanian citizenship provides very precise reasons and circumstances that can lead to the loss of citizenship. When the State is the one revoking citizenship, the criteria are very stringent. For example, if someone enters into service for an enemy state or for the military in a foreign country, there is just cause or valid grounds to revoke citizenship.

This document also outlines the experiences of some Jordanian citizens of Palestinian origin, which are undoubtedly related to what is referred to as Jordan's disengagement from citizens living in the West Bank. Article 2 of the instructions that were adopted states that all persons living in the West Bank prior to July 31, 1988, would not be Jordanian citizens, but would be considered Palestinian citizens.

This is a decision that I will render-the Human Rights Watch document states that people who lose their citizenship have recourse in Jordan. The High Court of Justice has rendered decisions; even though only a few people have appealed the decision to revoke their citizenship, some have appeared before this High Court of Justice in Jordan.

Human Rights Watch states: The lack of confidence in the courts may not be justified, as the High Court of Justice has ruled in several cases against the decisions to withdraw nationality ... In a 1997 decision, the court established that nationality cannot be withdrawn "except in accordance with the provisions of the law," and that "it is not allowed to revoke nationality on the basis of decisions that the [government] bureaucracy issues.3

On page 46 of this document, it is stated that, still according to the court, the fact that someone has a Palestinian passport and is in the West Bank for work does not affect their citizenship. In another decision rendered in 2000, the court even ruled that a child who has a Jordanian father is also Jordanian-even if the father subsequently renounced his Jordanian citizenship.

In another decision, in 1997, the court ruled that the connection between different colour-coded cards and loss of citizenship was not valid: "the court in the 1997 verdict also pronounced on the link between the color-coded cards and loss of nationality: 'Exchanging the yellow card (which grants nationality to the Jordanian) with a green card (which grants nationality to the Palestinian) does not revoke Jordanian nationality from the claimant as long as this exchange took place by way of the Follow-up and Inspection Department and did not occur according to his request or wish."4
It is certain that you will appeal this decision to the Federal Court.

I am basing my decision on the fact that, because of the aforementioned reasons, credibility was undermined. When the application for a permit was made, you stated that you had Jordanian citizenship, and the decision to grant the visa was based on that information. I read the documentation and I see that in Jordan-even if this does not happen often-it is possible to appear before the courts to appeal a decision to revoke citizenship.

I am taking the claimant's personal situation into account: his parents are XXXX and, according to what he told the immigration officer, they are Jordanian citizens; and there is no refugee protection claim against Jordan. I am of the opinion that, in Jordan, the claimant can appear before the courts and obtain his Jordanian citizenship once again.
I render this decision with complete respect for any dissenting opinion that could be presented, and that will certainly be presented to the Federal Court.
I conducted this analysis in keeping with my code of ethics as a member, based on the evidence, as well as a review of the claimant's testimony and the statements that he made previously.
So, this is my decision.

My conclusion is that the claimant has Jordanian citizenship. If he has lost his citizenship, he has recourse in Jordan and, since there is no refugee protection claim against Jordan, this puts an end to his refugee protection claim before me.

This is my decision. Having said that, I repeat, you have recourse. If I have committed an error, the Federal Court will ask us to reconsider it all eventually. Alain Bissonnette Me Alain Bissonnette December 1, 2010 Date IRB translation Original language: French REFUGEE PROTECTION DIVISION / ORAL DECISION / STATELESS / VISA / STUDENT / PASSPORT / NATIONALITY / RIGHT TO CITIZENSHIP / MALE / NEGATIVE / JORDAN 1 Exhibit A-4: Response ZZZ103109.E, July 8, 2009. 2 Exhibit A-3: National Documentation Package on Jordan, August 30, 2010, Tab 3.9: Human Rights Watch, February 2010, Stateless Again: Palestinian-Origin Jordanians Deprived of their Nationality, http://www.hrw.org/node/87906. 3 Supra, footnote 2: p. 45. 4 Supra, footnote 2: p. 46. --------------- --------------- --------------- --------------- RPD File No. / No de dossier de la SPR : MA8-08749 7
